Early In The Interview with Irwin Hirsch, Benjamin Wolstein considers the possibility that his analyst, Clara Thompson, acted as a conduit to her analyst, Sandor Ferenczi. Wolstein muses that his conceptualization of the psychoanalytic situation as “experiential field” was an inheritance of Ferenczi's “dialogue of the unconscious” and technique of mutual analysis via Thompson's concept of “direct psychoanalytic experience.”

Whatever the truth of Wolstein's musing in this regard, the vital dialogue between him and Hirsch that ensues affords the reader a remarkable window into the history and evolution of psychoanalytic praxis. Wolstein's career covers nearly a half-century of roiling change within a discipline that itself has only recently celebrated its first centennial.

Throughout the entire period of his work, Wolstein has been a radical and controversial originator of the very changes that today command center stage in the psychoanalytic debate. While Wolstein's fundamental tenet regarding the nature of the clinical enterprise may be a commonplace, if still controversial principle today—the analyst's use of his own experiences as the central phenomena in informing his interaction with his patient—Wolstein proposed it in the 1950s. Clearly, both as psychoanalytic thinker and clinician, Wolstein was way ahead of his time.

Wolstein, however, did not simply wait for the times to catch up with him. His ideas regarding the nature of the analyst's participation continue to be unique and radical, even in today's more receptive analytic atmosphere. Hence, this issue of Contemporary Psychoanalysis has gathered a number of eminent analysts from different schools to respond to his ideas. Their commentaries attest to the vitality of Wolstein's thinking in the contemporary psychoanalytic world, as well as to the controversy his ideas continue to inspire.

This Book is one of a series, the Library of Object Relations, that is meant to be a venue for new writers who employ diverse aspects of British, American, and international object relations theory. In his introduction, Gabbard identifies himself as a pluralist and an eclectic. He selects from the variety of psychoanalytic theories those he believes best serve the analyst in understanding and helping the patient in the analytic endeavor. He includes the ego psychology of David Rappaport, the South American and British Kleinians, the middle group of the British object relations school, the American relationalists, and those converging with the latter from the classical position. A major influence on him is Thomas Ogden, an American counterpart of the British middle school.

Against this background, Gabbard focuses on what he calls the “sea change” in conceptualization of the analytic relationship, from the prior view of the analyst as dispassionate observer of the patient's intrapsychic conflicts to a view wherein the analyst's full participation in the analytic relationship involves not only countertransference, but enactments.

In a Seminal Paper, the historian Joan Scott (1992) distinguished between two theoretical strategies that historians have utilized to bring marginalized voices into mainstream theory. The first, what I call the “conventional strategy,” assimilates previously silenced voices without questioning the basic foundations of historical theory. The inclusion of narrative accounts of women, gay men and lesbians, transsexual individuals, and people from “minority” groups into the record challenges historians’ability to maintain that there is one superior way of being human and that everything else is an aberration. A space for an intersubjectivity truly respectful of differences is opened.

Despite the fact that the conventional method leaves essentialist categories intact, its importance cannot be overemphasized. It has exposed the lies underlying hegemonic constructions, such as those that hold that white men are superior, that selves are coherent and unitary, that heterosexuality is the benchmark of “healthy” development, or that “femininity” and “masculinity” exist in nature.

In psychoanalysis, the pathbreaking work of Richard Isay (1989) serves as an illustration of the conventional strategy in the way that it broadens our view of what constitutes a healthy developmental trajectory, thereby granting gay men a legitimacy previously denied them by the psychoanalytic establishment. Yet, because Isay stays within the categories underlying psychoanalytic theory (e.g., man-woman, gay-straight), he unwittingly reproduces them.

What Karen Maroda appears to value above all is emotional honesty. This is what makes her book such compelling reading. I found it to be a courageous book clinically, filled with detailed, engaging accounts of work with several patients, any one of whom would try any analyst's skills, patience, and emotional range. Maroda sets the tone for the book in her introduction, stating that how she works reflects who she is; she presents her work as arising from personal “truths” that may be shared by some readers and not by others. Though I did not share all of her truths, I nonetheless found most to be quite compelling because of her straightforwardness and honesty.

To understand this book, it is important to understand something about Maroda's development as a psychoanalyst. A native of Milwaukee, she commuted to Chicago for “bootlegged training” at a time before psychologists were admitted to most institutes on equal footing with psychiatrists.

When I was Seven Years Old, I was seen as quite heroic by my four-year-old brother. He followed me around and, in general, proved to be a colossal pain in the neck. I did, nonetheless, always seek him out when the puppet show Rootie Kazootie appeared on our newly acquired television set. We watched happily until the caped villain, Poison Zumac, his mustache ominously curled, peeked out from the right side of the TV screen. My brother would shriek with fear and run to the comfort of our mother. I would charge after him and calmly explain that there was nothing to fear, because Poison Zumac was merely a puppet. I did not return to the show until I had gently coaxed him back.

My professed ability to recognize the difference between reality and make-believe undoubtedly enhanced my already idealized status. Some twenty years later, when my brother and I were reminiscing about this and other childhood experiences, he was stunned as I confessed that I followed him out of the room because I was terrified of being left alone with Poison Zumac.

In my role of older brother I felt safe and unafraid as long as my younger brother was in the room. I enjoyed both the TV program and my revered position. My fragile feeling of security was clearly tied to my dependence on my brother's presence. His fragile sense of safety was linked to his dependence on me.

From an interpersonal perspective, I carried the autonomy while my younger brother carried the dependence for the dyad. The balance was quickly altered once the “dependent” partner left the scene. Because my sense of esteem relied on his need to be comforted, I did not help him master his anxiety. That would have shifted our dynamic.

At the Same Time that I was reading Philip Bromberg's remarkable volume, I came across a review by Gary Wills called “Augustine's Remarkable Decade.” It is about Augustine's extraordinary work between the years 390 and 400. Concerning Augustine's writing, Wills stated something that captured for me the most interesting and enjoyable part of reading Bromberg's book, as well as his many papers: “We can watch the drama of his ideas as they emerge and struggle in his mind. The text does not deliver us a product, but calls us into a process.”

Bromberg, playful but unrelentingly, calls us into a process. Indeed, these are meditations in the best sense of the word. Bromberg takes familiar landscapes—clinical dilemmas, character phenomena, states of trauma and defensive adaptation—and tells us about his struggle and experience in a fresh, unique, and probing way. There are times when I want a product in reading, just as I sometimes do in conducting analysis. This may be something akin to wanting a patient to speak in a way that I might understand him. Yet patients don't do this in a straightforward way. Instead, Bromberg's felicitous phrase “Speak! that I may see you,” borrowed from Socrates, gets at the notion that anyone invited to say what comes to mind will also reveal, as it were, the person they wish to hide. Bromberg is able to inform us about who he and his patient are, while inviting us into a process in which we get a sense of the struggle in being seen.

The Heated Criticisms of Freud in recent years from writers such as Crews (1993), Fish (1989), Grünbaum (1984), and others, may be taken as signs of a much larger cultural rift than is manifest in

155

questions like whether psychoanalysis can claim to be a science, or why the seduction theory was abandoned. John Forrester, in the last and title chapter of Dispatches from the Freud Wars, engages the critics—whose remarks have sometimes strayed from the path of reasonableness—with specific historical evidence and informed interpretation; but what he really does is lift the discussion into the broader contemporary discourse about the nature of knowledge, of the individual person, and of concern for others. In Truth Games, Forrester examines the implications of the special condition of psychoanalytic technique for the authority of truth in a variety of practices. In two extended essays he fashions a chain of reasoning that links truth and lying to the obligations of social life implicit in debt and monetary exchange—obligations that are sometimes transcended through the pure act of giving. Throughout both books, the author demonstrates how Freud remains implicated in today's shifting foundations of epistemology and ethics, and especially in their ramifications for the autonomy and freedom of each individual citizen, patient, and psychoanalyst.

In both books, Forrester's approach relies and enlarges on Lacan's (1968, 1977, 1981) structuralist view of interpretation, Wittgenstein's (1958) understanding of language as practice, and Derrida's (1976) sometimes playful relativizing. His essays are neither standard histories nor philosophical treatises. Rather, as Forrester (1980) said in concluding an earlier book, “it will not be easy to find this work a disciplinary niche” (p. 211). Indeed, his interests, which focus most centrally on the cultural impact of Freud and psychoanalysis, are rather broad in scope, but his writing attends to the details: they may be as mundane as Freud's “grumpiness” in response to the reviewers of The Interpretation of Dreams, or as heady as the dilemmas confronted in propositional logic by modern attempts to establish an absolute ground for truth. Readers who believe that the final version of psychoanalytic theory has not yet been written might like these books; those who feel metapsychologically secure just might hate them, or maybe they'll be surprised.

I Found Irwin Hirsch's Interview with Ben Wolstein enormously inspiring. For me, Wolstein expresses the fundamental spirit of psychoanalysis: what attracted me to psychoanalysis in the first place; what I was disappointed to find all too rare, once I joined the ranks of our profession; and what I consider a sine qua non for the future of psychoanalysis as a therapeutic discipline.

Clearly, Wolstein was way ahead of his time. Perhaps Clara Thompson was, too. Wolstein certainly emphasizes that he's standing on her shoulders; but I suspect him of affectionately overestimating her contribution to his own development. For example, his approach to the problem of self-disclosure by an analyst is apparently significantly different from Thompson's. Wolstein describes how Thompson would acknowledge the importance of her personal reactions and their influential presence within the treatment, but declined to make them a subject for candid, explicit discussion with her patient. Wolstein tells that he teased her about her reticence; discussing it years later, he conveys the same playful acceptance he must have shown originally. Nonetheless, Wolstein's good-natured objection to Thompson's stance of privacy constitutes an enormously consequential critique of the way she—and many other analysts of varying theoretical orientations—set up the ground rules of the analytic relationship: “Tell me what you really think about me, but I'm not going to tell you what I really think about me. You show me yours, but I'm not going to show you mine.”

Part of what impresses me as precocious about Wolstein, of course, can be attributed to the whole Sullivanian movement that was formative for him. We know very well that the contributions of the interpersonalists went unrecognized by “mainstream Freudians” for decades, despite the fact that the interpersonalists anticipated concerns that are only now coming into focus for their colleagues. (Hirsch, among others, has documented this history in detail.) Even within a Sullivanian context, though, I find Wolstein particularly impressive.

William James, lecturing before the general public, is said to have likened the history of philosophy to a turtle standing on the back of another turtle. “But Professor James,” a member of the audience asked, “what is underneath the bottom turtle?” “Madam,” James replied, “it is turtles all the way down.”

The present article focuses on the contributions of Benjamin Wolstein within the theoretical evolution of the American school of interpersonal psychoanalysis. As with James's commentary on plumbing the depths of philosophy, one is well advised to proceed with humility in tracing the pathways of complex thought. How much more so when attempting to clarify Benjamin Wolstein's rich and densely packed intellectual trajectory from Sullivan's midcentury interpersonalism to the millennium's relationism. Wolstein had no conceptual difficulty with these labels. He saw them—like Dewey's (1896) foundational understanding of the reflex arc—as naturally transformational. He recognized that one concept flows into the other. In fact, each concept relies on the other. But where Dewey's arc follows the progress of a muscular nerve twitch, Wolstein's parallel arc transforms the intellectual history of twentieth-century American psychoanalysis. As Wolstein frequently noted, Harry Stack Sullivan's orientation had been the study of interpersonal relations. That “interpersonalists” from the start had lopped off “relationism” in describing their practice was a dialectical setup—a synthesis waiting to happen. “Relationism” necessarily completed “interpersonalism” by bringing explicitly to the consensual social field the joint operations of unique human need and desire. The painstakingly fastidious dialectical process that would integrate interpersona with psyche, public and private, within the joint therapeutic field spanned fifty years of Wolstein's professional life.

For the purpose of the present discussion, this timeline is divided into two sections.

This is an Indispensable book for those who want to understand the institutional life of contemporary psychoanalysis in this country. No one is better placed than Wallerstein to tell so much of the story of the antitrust lawsuit brought against the American Psychoanalytic and the International and what that reveals about their administrative structures, their relationship to each other, their cultures, and their guiding principles.

As a key member of the American's Committee on Training for Research, as well as a foremost researcher himself, Wallerstein not only knew firsthand the “lay” analysts admitted into research roles and the quandries and controversies surrounding them, but he participated in the frustrating internal efforts of the American to rectify this blatantly inequitable situation. Later, as president of the International, he was literally a party to the lawsuit and the negotiations leading to its settlement. He knew so many of the participants, he directly argued its central issues, and he is able to quote from a treasure trove of original documents.

Moreover, Wallerstein generously weaves into his account the story of his own professional development, making it possible for the reader to understand better the cultural and professional climate in which these controversies were played out. Tellingly, for example, he describes how he was turned down in his application to the New York Psychoanalytic because, as his well-placed supporters were able to determine, “the chastening effect of being rejected on a first application and having to reapply could be helpful to my emotional maturation” (p. 90).

Finally, Wallerstein brings to his task a broad intellectual framework for placing the issues.

Stuart Pizer, who also builds trust by not evading what alienates him, takes us further into the meanings of such psychic interplay between patient and therapist. He views the coconstruction of authentically shared reality as an essential aspect of evoking change. In this spirit he begins the treatment of a poignantly schizoid man, Donald, by injecting his own solution to the problem of being unable to tolerate the patient's body odor: he confronts the man with the presence of his smell. When the patient agreed to use deodorant, Pizer responded to this first “negotiation” as a sign that he would be able to commit himself to working with him in treatment. And so begins an interaction that leads to the patient's developing the emotional closeness for which he has always longed. Pizer notes his awareness that in giving the patient the pseudonym “Donald,” he has imbued his memory with a bit of the inspiring closeness he has felt for the writings of Donald Winnicott. His approach to Donald profoundly respects Winnicott's paradox that “it is a joy to be hidden but disaster not to be found.”

Echoing Pizer's dedication to connecting inner and outer worlds, the book contains two sections. Part I deals with the negotiation of paradox within the consulting room as a conceptual bridge between analyst and patient. Part II extends the horizon of the view from that bridge to high-light how similar processes of empathic connection or disconnection frame negotiations within wider social circles of gender, nations, and species. Here Pizer considers those damaging and polarized representations of distinctions in identity (gender categories, national differences, and so forth) which, rife with projection and the need for dominance, bespeak an intolerance for paradox and negotiation. The goal of developing ways to synthesize multiplicity and paradox within an identity that is valued (by individual and social group) is the unifying theme of the book.

Among Today's interpersonally trained analysts, the terms “coconstructed,” “intersubjective,” and “two person” are addendums to lettered credentials. Countertransference saturates many consulting rooms, even across different “schools” of psychoanalytic thinking (Gabbard, 1995). Aron and Anderson's edited volume, however, brings innovation to what has become nothing short of mainstream, because it considers the historically intrapsychic, private body as inextricably bound to the other.

If Freud took the flesh and its urges as the base of a theory of all inner life, Aron ambitiously counters with his own theory of psychosomatic organization and psychoanalytic cure. Writing the first chapter, he patterns a fabric of ideas using the general theme of the “reflexive mind,” or the capacity to move back and forth between the self as subject and as object. Like many before him (Aron credits Jung, Krystal, Blatt, Bach, and Fonagy, to name but a few), he values holding the tension between one's subjectivity and the perspective of the other as pivotal to psychic vitality. In its absence there is a deficiency in awareness, management, and expression of one's own experience, and also an inability to appreciate and utilize people.

Within this fabric, Aron weaves the thread of the body, believing that the foundation for the capacity for self-reflexivity lies in our bodily sensations. Inspired by the work of Eigen, Aron takes as an example the act of breathing, a concrete model of “ego cohesion and interaction” (p. 23). At what point, he invites us to consider, is one's breath a part of the self, and at what point is it a part of the air, the outside? In developing self-reflexivity, then, it is imperative that the body self bump up against the external world and what is outside, without forsaking what is inside.

Here is the notion of an integrated identity developing intersubjectively, and Aron's mapping of it explains the current deemphasis on positivist interpretation, the limits of which have rarely been so elegantly and clearly argued.

The Real-Life Relationships of most intimates usually reiterate familiar patterns, those intricately layered interactional loops we inhabit, just as we inhabit “home” without “seeing it” as the outsider does. We evolve the patterns as developmental exigencies call forth changes. We have little awareness of their scope, architecture, and intricacy, or how they shape us as we cocreate and coperpetuate them. This mutual shaping is the familiarness of intimacy, the fluent enactment of knowing we belong. Even when the familiar is chronically painful, as in especially rigidified interactional patterns, we cannot get outside of what we don't know; we cannot change our participations in their endless replays to make them different enough for new possibilities to emerge. And so we live in deep and multiple binds that tie in ways but dimly grasped by us as partners in intimacy, as parents and children and siblings.

Family therapists aim to interfere with the way those binds are perpetuated. Their goal is to allow the ties to generate and accommodate new and growth-facilitating interactional patterns. Gerson's unique book introduces psychoanalysts to the perspectives of the family therapist in a way that illuminates what the therapeutic levers are made of and why they are placed where they are; but it also compares how the very same clinical problem might be seen and addressed from a psychoanalytic perspective.

Gerson's guide for psychoanalysts to couple and family therapy's world of theory and praxis contrasts demarcated psychoanalytic and systemic paradigms in mutually illuminating figure-ground relationship. Gerson shows how the dynamic understanding of a clinical problem from either perspective enriches the other, rather than excluding, subordinating, or rendering the other meaningless. Her extended presentations of clinical material demonstrate varieties of interventions and their rationales.

When I was Young, my psychologist-psychoanalyst father told me psychologists study “what makes people tick.” I was fascinated. My father's phrase made the world open up to me in a new way. My experience, it turns out, was not unique. Almost every author in this book—a series of autobiographical essays by psychotherapists of various persuasions about their career choices—at some point uses the word “fascination” to describe discovery of and excitement about the subject matter of the mental health disciplines.

The almost ecstatic tone of the essays is striking. For the most part, these writers love their work. They are thrilled to have found it. They feel they have hit the jackpot. The work of psychotherapy is satisfying on so many levels: intellectually, it is the highly stimulating study of the mind (the ultimate subject matter); emotionally, it affords continual intense and deeply intimate interactions with other people and with oneself (in conditions of relative safety and control)

In this First Chapter, Axelrod recognizes that “As clinicians, we have no models of mature working to guide us as we do varied and sophisticated models of mature loving” (p. 1). This predicament is hardly an accident, given the particular pastiche of ideas and clinical practices to which the author limits himself, calling it “my version of the analytic ideal.” Actually it is a popular enough combination of concepts and clinical practices, including old standbys like the Oedipus complex, psychic determinism, and object relations theory, with a dash of other familiar favorites. The absence of a model of maturity is at least partly the result of the retention of notions of human development that understand maturity as little more than an extrapolation from the childhood past. This also fails to explain, for instance, what differentiates us from those of our prehistoric ancestors who also had good-enough mothers.

Despite this kind of theoretical limitation, Axelrod has taken pains to inform himself about management theory and has even familiarized himself with business settings. The result is a book that may well prove acceptable and useful to those analysts of a similarly conservative stripe. Particularly addressed to this audience is his final chapter on “The Psychology of a Changing Workplace.” It is concise, well written, and underscores how today's changing technology has altered the climate of business practice. In this connection he pays particular attention to a current management strategy that has especially troublesome psychological consequences. It is the spread of downsizing, that is, dismissal of a large subdivision of employees for reasons of profitability, and without regard for their individual merits. In its current version, downsizing confronts all levels of employees with an ever-present threat of job loss.

It would have made excellent sense to put this chapter earlier in the book, in order to enrich information about working conditions relevant to the author's fourteen case histories.

The Collapse Of The Third In A Fee-For-Service Structure*

Linda Miller JD and Jean Twomey PHD

Jean Twomey

18 Bellevue Avenue
Cambridge, MA 02140

Jean Twomey   investigator in psychiatry and human behavior, Brown University School of Medicine; research associate, Infant Development Center, E. P. Bradley Hospital, East Providence, Rhode Island.

Certain Conceptual Problems are inherent in doing psychodynamic psychotherapy within the typical fee-for-service setting, a structure that has become increasingly common in the provision of outpatient psychotherapy services. Although there is a growing body of psychoanalytic literature on a number of issues involved in managed care as it affects the practice of psychodynamic psychotherapy, we have found no analytic discussion regarding a different aspect of the changing culture of the mental health care system in this country: namely, the shift from salaried to fee-for-service positions for clinicians practicing in outpatient clinics. Decisions by mental health clinics to pay the therapist in this manner are made for purposes of cost-savings and survival in an increasingly competitive marketplace. The particular clinical and theoretical implications of that arrangement for a psychodynamic treatment have not, to our knowledge, been examined.

We consider the structural and dynamic dilemmas in fee-for-service practice with respect to the presence of what is commonly termed the Third in analytic work, and highlight the problematic place of the therapist in relation to the analytic space and its frame. The problems we discuss here are most clearly seen in the circumstance of the absent patient, the missed appointment. We illuminate and give life to that issue through a clinical vignette. Because the flaws that we identify relate to the analytic space and to the context that holds the dyad, however, such problems are not limited to particular clinical circumstances, but simply manifest themselves most obviously in relation to the missed session.

For a number of reasons, this topic is significant to practitioners and supervisors of psychodynamic psychotherapy. Some of those reasons we mention here without elaboration, but not because they are insignificant.

We wish to thank Robert Adelberg, Ed.D., for his insightful reading of this article and his support during its writing. We dedicate this article to our brothers.

Studies of Symbolic Thinking encompass widespread fields of inquiry in philosophy, linguistics, and mythology. My interest in this broad subject lies in the psychoanalytic understanding of the use of symbols in borderline and schizophrenic psychopathology. The concept of symbol use refers to freedom from concrete thinking that permits the abstract investment of commonplace feelings and experience with imaginative, linguistic significance. Both schizophrenic and borderline individuals with signs of thought disorder rely on forms of concrete thinking that indicate limitations in distinguishing differences between the literal and the metaphorical. Schizophrenic patients with a florid thought disorder reveal greater lapses in abstraction ability and a psychotic use of symbols in which language may lose its communicative value.

The eradication of psychological boundaries in psychotic identity disturbance is commensurate with the far-reaching relinquishment of the ability to differentiate internal from external, self from other, and human from nonhuman. The concept of identity disturbance thus signifies either the lack of distinction between self and nonself, or the erosion of one's conviction about possessing a clearly delineated, personal human identity. The term “identity loss” reflects relatively severe forms of each type of identity disturbance. In some psychosis-prone borderline and schizophrenic personalities, reality-testing impairments are accompanied not only by deteriorations in symbolic thinking, but by delusional beliefs about the absence of a discrete, permanent human identity and the presence of a partially animal or other nonhuman identity. Although fantasies about becoming an animal are common in childhood and in totemic societies, there has been relatively little psychoanalytic literature concerning delusional beliefs about being part animal. Such concrete, presymbolic thinking involves underlying relational patterns of primitive anxiety.

In a World-War-II-Vintage Book titled See Here, Private Hargrove there is a passage that has always delighted me. It deals with a sergeant's effort to elicit from a new recruit the knowledge of and compliance with a numbered order, whereby any untoward occurrence requires calling for the officer of the day. It goes something like this: “Suppose you see a battleship coming over that dune; what are you going to do?” Without batting an eyelash the private replies, “I'll take a torpedo and sink it.” “And where, may I ask, would you find that torpedo?” inquires the sergeant testily. “In the same place that you found your goddam battleship,” says the private glowingly.

Irreverent though it may sound, this memory sprang to my mind, and I do not believe it is irrelevant to the things I was preparing to say in reflective response and appreciative appraisal of Irwin Hirsch's painstaking interview of Benjamin Wolstein. This is because, among these things, I consider the anxiety of influence; the creative use of immediate experience; the trust in something that one knows when it happens, despite the difficulty in defining it; the presence of the absent until the latter arrives; the unique as an affirmation of something at the exclusion of anything else; the intimations of “immaculate perception” and objectless love; and the belief in a sine qua non for psychoanalysis leading to a most exacting but elusive legacy. If there had been any questions as to where the Wolstein opus stands, or how the man saw himself, their impossibility and possibilities live on.

It is of interest that the interview begins with questions about influences, and “strong influences” at that. Though it is implicit in the response, I was intrigued that the fact that Clara Thompson was Wolstein's analyst and not a supervisor does not get clarified till a bit later. It made me wonder, for the umpteenth time, how we conceive of influences in psychoanalytic training and practice. Do we have any inclinations, let alone reasons, to believe—or at least, hypothesize—that such influences occur more prevalently in a supervisory or didactic situation than in the analytic one? Could it be the other way around?

Irwin Hirsch   faculty and supervisor, Manhattan Institute for Psychoanalysis; professor of psychology and supervisor, Postdoctoral Program in Psychotherapy and Psychoanalysis, Adelphi University; distinguished visiting faculty, William Alanson White Institute; adjunct clinical professor, Department of Psychiatry, Mt. Benjamin Wolstein Was interviewed on two consecutive Saturday afternoons in May 1998, in his office in New York City. The interviews totalled almost six hours and were audio taped and subsequently transcribed. This abridged version represents well less than one-half of the original transcript. Among what is not included is the early part of the interview. This segment dealt with Wolstein's family background and some of his significant personal and educational experiences prior to entering analytic training.

IH: Who would you say were your strongest influences?

BW: My major influence, obviously, was Clara Thompson. I'll always have deep affection and regard for her. She took me on a trip and I took her on a trip. It was a quest for psychic freedom, you know. In that context, anything went. Of course, we had differences of opinion; I mean, about the question of countertransference and how to work with it. This made our differences real. She used to take the established position of the early 1950s—“that belongs in my analysis, not in yours.” Of course, I was a bit of a wiseacre. I used to ask her, “if it belongs in your analysis, what is it doing in mine?” She didn't get defensive about it. She laughed. And eventually, something I'll always respect her for, we began to do a certain amount of open analysis. I began to realize how her psychology actually affected some of the work that went on between us. And I thought that was extraordinary for the time. Later, I began to develop the idea about the interlocking of transference and countertransference, and wrote a monograph on countertransference in 1959. There, I also first described the experiential field of therapy. And I got a lot of it from my own experience working both with Clara and with patients. Not all my supervisors went for it. Some appeared to, but really didn't. But I already knew after Transference (1954) that the observations of transference and countertransference were interchangeable, no matter how a particular therapist and patient actually worked with them.

As We Come to The Close of the twentieth century and prepare to embark on a new one, I am tempted to reflect on the monumental and even catastrophic change that our world has suffered over the course of this century. Advances in technology have made it possible to raise the standard of living for many human beings, especially in Europe and North America, to heights that were unimaginable when our century began. Technology also brought us to the brink of destruction when the unbridled arms race between the United States and the Soviet Union took us to the precipice of nuclear war.

Yet, for all their potential for danger, the greatest threat that faces us today is not war or even the famine and poverty that many continue to suffer; indeed, it is those of us who appear to be protected from such horrors that have the most to lose. What we are in danger of losing is not the material comforts to which we are accustomed, but something much closer to our intrinsic humanity. I am thinking about the fragile condition of what was once taken for granted: our capacity to experience.

This may sound strange when, after all, our capacity to experience is something we generally take for granted. We invoke this term every day with such frequency that we seldom give it a second thought. Yet philosophers have written voluminous treatises on the nature of experience, and many psychoanalysts have even included the term in the titles of their books, including Wilfried Bion (Learning from Experience, 1962, Experiences in Groups, 1959); Neville Symington (The Analytic Experience, 1986); Thomas Ogden (The Primitive Edge of Experience, 1989); and R. D. Laing (The Politics of Experience, 1967; The Voice of Experience, (1982).

I am indebted to Prof. Martin Jay for his lecture presentation, “The Crisis of Experience in a Post-Subjective Age” (1998), that served as the inspiration for this essay. The following is an expansion of my discussion of Prof. Jay's presentation, which was in turn presented as the Keynote Address at the Annual Conference of the Instituto de Investigacion en Psicologia Clinica y Social, Mexico City, February 27, 1999.

We were in what seemed to me to be a particularly productive phase of the treatment. At long last (from my point of view) the patient was recognizing narcissistic aspects of her character that had hampered her in developing an enduring relationship. At thirty-five she was, I felt, really ready, for the first time, to engage in a deepening intimacy. Her whole life had been a momentous, courageous struggle with physical disabilities. Now she seemed ready to emerge more fully from the constraints of her psychological limitations. It was over the weekend that I got the message that she had suddenly died.

My experience of losing this patient was extremely painful, but I know I am hardly unique in having sustained such a loss. How do we bear these losses? What effects do they have over time, on our personal and professional lives?

Of course, the loss of a patient is usually less dramatic than this example. Patients terminate treatment, sometimes abruptly, sometimes with measured preparation. What is the accumulated impact on us, over the years, of living through so many endings? How can we best bear the sorrows that accompany a life in this rather peculiar profession?

Describing some peculiarities of the analytic relationship, especially in its termination phase, Nina Coltart (1996) writes,

The totality of the ending, which seems to go against the grain of all our work on love, loyalty, object-constancy, and intimacy, is reinforced by the austere prescription of no social contact thereafter. Thus we create an arbitrary situation that has much in common with a death. [p. 151]

This description is no less apt for the analyst than for the patient. We take it for granted that over the years we will suffer the loss of countless people who have been our partners in an intimate emotional exchange. However we lose contact with these people, the loss is usually total and final.

77

About Forty Years ago, Lancelot Law Whyte (1960), in his book The Unconscious Before Freud, wrote:

There is no one Zeitgeist, no single state of awareness in any community, even in a small professional group, at any one time. There may be traditional elements in decline, a variety of dominant elements, and new ones emerging…. Moreover, ideas may undergo cycles of influence, and may be temporarily inhibited, and consciously or unconsciously, transformed…. [O]nly the greatest ideas or men can continue to be fertile in the new context which they have themselves helped to create. [p. 12]

Whyte's contention was that the “unconscious mind” is such an idea, and that Sigmund Freud was such a man, but that “the antithesis conscious/unconscious may have exhausted its utility” (p. 174). “The trouble,” he says, “is not that they are ambiguous; that might be overcome by providing better definitions. It is that we do not yet know the right definitions to use, the meanings which would throw most light on the structure of mental processes. What we need is not merely words with definitions using other words, but insight into the changing structure of mental processes” (p. 15).

To underscore his argument about there being no single zeitgeist at any point in intellectual history, Whyte quotes H. A. Taine, a French historian who, as far back as 1871, questioned the idea of separating conscious and unconscious into different realms.

Early versions of sections of this essay were presented at the Fall 1998 meeting of The American Psychoanalytic Association as part of a panel entitled “Have We Changed Our View of the Unconscious in Contemporary Clinical Work?” and at the February 2000 meeting of the PEP-CD ROM Conference, “Journeys on the Royal Road: Current Perspectives on the Clinical Use of Dreams.”685

Years ago, Loewenstein (1957) suggested that the analyst should act as if theory didn't exist. This extreme position—perhaps only possible for an analyst so secure in his theory that he cannot distinguish it from fact—nonetheless echoes a persistent theme in our literature. We must try not only to avoid suggesting to the patient what he thinks or feels, but we must try to avoid prefiguring for ourselves what we will come to understand. We need an open mind.

There are many expressions of this idea, a kind of clinical common sense. Freud himself wrote to Ferenczi: “one should not make theories—they must fall into one's house as uninvited guests while one is occupied with the investigation of detail” (Falzeder & Brabant, 1996, p. 74). But as we also know, Freud made theory into shibboleths, a basis for professional warfare. The battlefield of psychoanalytic history is littered with the corpses of those theoretical conflicts. It may be, as Cooper (1997) and Weinshel (1990) have argued, that we have matured to the point where we can now profit from our theoretical diversity, but that has not simplified the problem of the relation between theory and practice.

Indeed, with the growing plurality of theoretical schools, as well as the postpositivist turn in our thinking about theory itself and its relation to truth, there is a new urgency about our relation to the observational data of psychoanalysis. On one hand, we cannot presume any definitively correct theoretical framework. Even if we are ourselves persuaded about the truth of our own particular orientation, we are forced to be modest about its claim on reality. Respectable and accepted practitioners hold to different theoretical orientations (see Hamilton, 1997). This is the lesson of pluralism. On the other hand, we are increasingly forced to recognize that the facts, the data themselves, are always imbued with meaning. That is, there is no clear distinction to be made between facts and theories; there is no place to stand apart from our theories.

My First Response to reading the interview of Benjamin Wolstein by Irwin Hirsch was to feel sorry that I had not read Wolstein's works more studiously and recognized him as he deserved to be recognized. I barely recall reading some of his papers many years ago, no doubt giving up too early because of the density of his writing and lack of case material. Paralleling my regret at not giving him his due, I am pleased to see the publication of this interview because it opens a window to the world of Wolstein's deep and humane conceptions of the relational analytic situation. Not burdened by having to write, and aided by Hirsch's penetrating questions, Wolstein the man, the analyst, and the very plain-speaking advocate for mutuality is revealed. His humility in the face of Hirsch's admiration, his refusal to create any “rules,” and his steadfast belief that each therapeutic relationship is unique create a portrait of a man who accepted his position as facilitator of the patient's experience, not mover and shaker, and certainly not standard-bearer. He said he was not into theory building or telling other people how to work, implicitly stating that he had no interest in providing anything that people could use to defend their behavior in relation to patients. He didn't want analysts to be like him, he wanted them to become themselves and help their patients to do the same.

Despite Hirsch's many questions on this front, Wolstein brushes aside any notions that we, as analysts, will exert undue influence on our patients if we are forthcoming about our personal experience. If anything, he seemed to become ever-so-slightly impatient with this line of questioning, as if to say to Hirsch, “No, we are not on the same track. It's not a question of influence. If we influence them or fail to influence them in any way, it is because they are seeking that influence. They take what they can, or refuse it. It is their experience.” The issue for Wolstein was authenticity rather than influence.

Of Course, Many of us are familiar with the opening lines of Dr. Seuss's classic The Cat in the Hat. In recalling how, as a first-year analytic candidate, I approached supervision, it seems particularly apt. I remember my feelings and anxieties well—this was serious business! I had a control case and a supervisor who was both a supervising and training analyst at a prestigious psychoanalytic institute, and who initially seemed to be forbidding and solemn. And yet, as I became immersed in the work, I began to consider—was it in fact no time for play? Certainly, like those two children in Seuss, there was work to be done: my learning, the patient's treatment, and the supervisor's teaching. But how exactly was this to occur? In Recent Years, postmodern and relational schools of psychoanalysis have been greatly influenced by Sullivan's constructivist concept of the self. Sullivan (1936-37, 1950) claimed that a belief in our unique individuality is a delusion. He exploded the myth of a person as a single self, proposing that we have as many personalities as interpersonal relations, thereby anticipating the postmodernist movement in psychoanalysis with its emphasis on the decentered, multiple self. According to Sullivan (1950), “no such thing as the durable, unique, individual personality is ever clearly justified. For all I know every human being has as many personalities as he has interpersonal relations” (pp. 219-220). The “over-weening conviction of authentic individual selfhood … amounts to a delusion of unique individuality” (Sullivan, 1936-37, p. 16).

Although this aspect of Sullivan's theory freed us to examine our multiplicity as persons, it also raised questions regarding our unity, an area that remains relatively unformulated in interpersonal theory. Lionells (1999) has referred to this as the problem of the independent psychic existence in the midst of psychological flux. If there is multiplicity, is unity in the person merely an illusion? Benjamin Wolstein was one of the most prolific writers of his generation of psychoanalysts, and certainly the most prolific interpersonal psychoanalyst. He wrote seven books and about 100 articles and chapters in books. He was a regular speaker at New York University, William Alanson White Institute, Adelphi, Institute for Contemporary Psychoanalysis, and Manhattan Institute for Psychoanalysis, but he rarely spoke at other psychoanalytic institutes. There were several early forays into mixed psychoanalytic audiences, but over the years they were fewer and fewer,1 while some of his colleagues (Levenson in his generation, and Blechner, Ehrenberg, Greenberg, and Mitchell, to name but a few, in the next) continued to broaden their audience. Wolstein trained several generations of analysts as their analyst, supervisor, or teacher. The names of his students who claim him as a major influence reads like a Who's Who of interpersonal and relational psychology: Lewis Aron, Roanne Barnett, Tony Bass, Mark Blechner, Barbara Dusansky, Darlene Ehrenberg, Dan Epstein, John Fiscalini, Roberta Held-Weiss, Irwin Hirsch, Irena Klenbort, Phyllis Meshover, Ian Miller, Richard Rubens, Sue Shapiro, Clark Sugg, Warren Wilner, to name several. But outside this immediate circle of New York-based, interpersonally trained analysts, Wolstein's name and work are relatively unknown. Interpersonal Psychoanalysis is ideally suited to understanding and facilitating change in adult survivors of sexual abuse. From its inception with Harry Stack Sullivan, interpersonal psychoanalytic theory has emphasized the crucial impact of interactions and relationships on character and self-development. With its focus on anxiety and dissociation (e.g., the “not-me”), Sullivan's theory can be viewed as a theory of trauma. Contemporary interpersonal writers have further developed our understanding of the impact of dissociative processes. Sexual abuse is relationally based in its occurrence and the ways in which survivors process it. Interpersonal psychoanalysis, with its emphasis on the two-person collaborative model, allows the adult survivor to analyze and process the abuse memories and their aftereffects in a here-and-now relationship in which the subjectivity of each participant affects the other.

The interest in childhood sexual abuse and its effects emerged as a result of the confluence of several developments. The feminist movement heightened awareness of the victimization of women. This included focusing attention on how childhood sexual abuse and its aftereffects impacted on the development of the feminine self. At the same time, many Vietnam veterans were found to be experiencing surprisingly enduring and disruptive aftereffects of the war that were understood as posttraumatic stress. Also, some clinical thinkers “rediscovered” the importance of Freud's “seduction theory” and questioned its abandonment a hundred years ago (Herman, 1981; Masson, 1984; Miller, 1984). What began to come to awareness from practice and research was an appreciation of the similar symptoms of all trauma survivors. This resulted in a body of work known as trauma theory. Our practice with adult survivors of sexual abuse is informed by this theory.

Psychoanalytic Couple Therapy Extends the reach of psychoanalysis. In analysis, the analysand takes his or her enlarged self-understanding back into the outside world. Interactions there are modified by changes that have taken place in the analysis. The data base in the consulting room is the analysand's report. Even a verbatim quote is vulnerable to the flaws of memory and is selected for reasons that may be conscious or unconscious. In couple therapy, an important segment of the outside world is observed directly by the therapist. The importance of such observation is an extension of the current emphasis on the interactional quality of psychoanalysis or, as Gerson (1996) asserts, “What we are is determined by whom we are with, not in internal dialogue but in actual ‘external' relationships” (p. 64).

The goals of analysis cannot be achieved with a third party present. It is a method carefully structured to focus the conscious mind on exploring what is unconscious. The realities of the patient's life are relevant to this exploration. No matter how conscientiously analyst and analysand try to be objective in their understanding, however, they are both partisan and on the same side. In work with couples and families one must deal directly with part of the world outside the patient's own descriptions. Psychoanalytically informed couple therapy looks at unconscious forces that alter and distort the explicit communications of the participants.

In daily life, words and actions are affected by forces that are not conscious to the participants. Over time, as people get to know each other, they learn how to work through or around enough of these issues that life can go on. Couples who come to our offices are generally stymied by areas of conflict and misunderstanding that have not yielded to the ordinary modes of conflict resolution. Discussions become repetitive and circular, with no progress toward solutions or peace or acceptance.

Conversation in daily life is evanescent and unrecorded.

Psychoanalysis is both a collection of ideas and a method based on those ideas whose goal is the right way to live. Hence, psychoanalysis is an “ethic” in the sense that it concerns the manner by which individuals conduct themselves. Derived from the Greek ethike tekhne, meaning “the moral art,” ethike is in turn derived from the Greek ethos, meaning “character.” Both the character of a person who aspires to behave ethically and the customs of a people by which one's standards are measured derive from the concept. Morality, a subsidiary of ethics, pertains to distinctions between right and wrong and good and bad, whereas ethics, according to the Greeks, concerns the pursuit of happiness, the nature of which produces a state of equanimity by obtaining freedom from mental anguish.

If psychoanalysis is an ethic whose goal is liberation from psychic conflict, then the nature of that conflict must have something to do with the way one lives, thinks, and behaves. Although the character of an individual is no doubt decisive in the outcome of a patient's treatment, the psychoanalytic experience essentially revolves around a kind of work that is performed and accomplished, the outcome of which succeeds or fails. By analyzing the customs of a given patient—the manner by which that person lives—that patient is in a better position to change what needs to be changed and discover a better life. Ever Since Freud abandoned hypnosis, classical analysts have tried to eliminate, or at least reduce, the power of suggestion in their work. In theory, at least, change has traditionally been best achieved through insight and understanding the patient achieves via the analysis, and the undoing of resistance or defenses. Knowledge derived from analysis of the patient's conflicted mental life, particularly as these conflicts play out in the transference-countertransference, leads to the reduction of neurotic suffering. Over the years, technical recommendations such as maintaining neutrality, interpreting from surface to depth, and establishing a working alliance, were intended to minimize the analyst's power and influence (Josephs, 1997). The Patient, an engineer in his early forties, customarily greeted my appearance in the waiting room with, “Are you ready for me?” Until recently, how analysts understood and responded to such a question regarding the reality of the analyst's subjective state would not be controversial. The well-trained, well-analyzed analyst would be quite ready. Not so the patient, who, in expressing insecurity about the analyst's emotional accessibility, most likely would be communicating his own anxiety.

Traditionally, our options were clear and stress-free. The analyst might merely acknowledge the communication as a commonplace greeting, like saying “hello,” respond to the question with a question, “What makes you ask?” or, as I did, remain silent, note the remark inwardly, and wait to see what develops.

The development of a session and of a treatment, however, involves not only the analyst's “waiting” for the patient, but tolerating anxiety and allowing one's own emotions to cohere and contribute to the meaning of the psychoanalytic situation. This viewpoint takes us a distance from Freud's (1912) recommendation to put aside emotions and achieve “psycho-analytic purification” (p. 116). Contemporary analysts (e.g., Aron, 1996; Gerson, 1996; Jacobs, 1991) have argued convincingly that the “myth of ‘analyst without anxiety or anger’” (Racker, 1968) is not possible, or even desirable (Renik, 1996). Loewald (1986) declared the analyst's technique involves a “special trained ability to use his own love-hate in the service of analyzing” (p. 286).

Rather than eschew personal emotionality, in fact, the analyst must embrace it. This is a painful task, not easily achieved or sustained. Bion (1974) characterized analysis involving “two rather frightened people; the patient and the psychoanalyst. If there are not, one wonders why they are bothering to find out what everyone knows” (p. 13). The suggestion is not that the analyst primarily was afraid of the patient, but of realizing unrealized thought and emotion.

At Some Point during his interview with Irwin Hirsch, Benjamin Wolstein said that he views his clinical approach to psychoanalysis as being compatible with all other clinical analytic approaches. Yet his views, which Dr. Hirsch has skillfully and tenaciously helped to elucidate, are so radical, so startling when juxtoposed against other psychoanalytic positions, that one wonders how he could have claimed this. His position, as stated, is remarkable enough. When its implications are more fully drawn out, it becomes revolutionary. In an interview with Wolstein conducted by Gladys Guarton (1998), he said that he was interested in changing the basic nature of the field of psychoanalysis. This intention is apparent in the present interview.

To begin with, consider the implications of his views on resistance as applied to the act of an analytic therapist trying to listen to a patient. According to him, resistance against something or someone arises from a more fundamental concern: trying to adapt to the environmental surround. One is here attending more, for example, to another than to one's own experience. The purpose of resistance, he said, is also to effect a sense of separateness from the outside, and resisting another is one means of accomplishing this.

Listening focally to a patient's story, complaints, wishes, feelings, or thoughts reinforces the perception of the patient as being distinct from oneself. Furthermore, the therapist listens in order to be able to adapt to and form a relationship with the patient. Therefore, any effort to get a distinct sense of the patient becomes, in Wolstein's thinking, a form of counterresistance! Actually, the therapist may not be trying to resist something that the patient is attempting to do (e.g., influence the therapist's thoughts or feelings in a particular way). Rather, the very act of attending focally in an objectivistic way to the other creates the phenomenological reality of self and other to which one then tries to adapt.

Some Of The Most Moving emotional moments in life are experienced in silence: joy, enlightenment, tranquility, and the blissful feeling of being in love, to name a few. Along a similar line, some of life's other poignant moments are experienced in a different kind of silence: grief, loneliness, and despair. Silence can communicate yes or it can mean no. It can say everything or reveal nothing.

Silence in the analytic space has received its own worthy measure of investigation. In the analytic hour, silence takes on many different shades and tones. It may mean many different things for each patient and, in turn, for each analyst. It can encompass layers of thoughts and affects. As Freud (1915) concluded, it can serve as resistance to transference thoughts or as resistance to remembering and even repeating. Silence in the analytic space may also be an unconscious reenactment of a historical event, or a projective identification. It can serve as communication for needed space or an invitation for greater compassion. Silence in psychoanalysis has been thought to create a closed circle in treatment (Zeligs, 1961). It has also been emphasized as a response to object loss or as an acting out. There are those, such as Nacht (1964), who view silence as a reexperience of the perfect and total union at the preobject phase of development, while there are those such as Greenson (1961), who view silence as an empowering sense of a patient's means for retaining integrity. Silence has also been suggested to be the process toward verbalization and the securing of insight (Lowenstein, 1956). As Jacob Arlow (1961) so elegantly said, silence in treatment is different from any other kinds of silences. In silence, there lie psychic riches, as the case below reveals.

It has been More than Fifty Years since Harry Stack Sullivan suffered a fatal illness while on a mission for the World Health Organization. Members of the Washington School of Psychiatry, founded by Sullivan and a group of colleagues in 1936, initiated a commemorative conference under joint sponsorship with the William Alanson White Institute, which became the intellectual home of interpersonal psychoanalysis, based on his ideas. It is instructive to return to Sullivan's seminal writings with a view to considering how they have been expanded, revised, reinterpreted, and sometimes discarded in the exciting ferment of contemporary psychoanalytic theorizing. With this in mind, I offer this essay, which sketches the trajectory of Sullivan's central premises and suggests certain lines that might be pursued in the creation of a new, more comprehensive psychoanalytic paradigm. In the course of this discussion, certain distinctions are drawn between Sullivan's ideas and those of Freud and others who were writing at the same time. Interpersonal ideas are presented in opposition to orthodox theory, in order to highlight the historical perspective under consideration. There is the possibility that such a comparison might be read as maintaining the polarity between the interpersonal and Freudian schools. That is not my intention and certainly not my goal. In truth, such polarity hardly exists any longer. Contemporary theorists from all groups are considering common questions and finding common solutions. Indeed, I hope my essay will be read as searching for certain central positions that I believe are crucial for a new, integrative psychoanalytic paradigm.

Last year I participated in an ecumenical gathering, sponsored by the journals of the PEP-CD-ROM. My mother visited while I was writing my paper, and, as only a mother can, she asked how my business was doing, because she had read that managed care threatened to eliminate our fees. I tried to reassure her that this is really an exciting time to be an analyst.

The Exchange between Jay Frankel (1998 a, b) and Irwin Hirsh (1998) in this journal has raised many questions concerning the influence of the founding members of the William Alanson White Institute on contemporary interpersonal and relational psychoanalysis. In the exchange and in ensuing commentary, Fromm's clinical approach has been described by Frankel as authoritative, direct, confrontational, and focusing on the here and now at the expense of analyzing the significance of past experience. Hirsh notes that Fromm appealed to the patient's sense of realism and vitality, in order to mobilize a sense of urgency. Joining this exchange, Mitchell (1999) believes Fromm had a strong bias toward seeing dependence as regressive and pathological. All three authors acknowledge Fromm's important contribution to relational approaches by his emphasis on authenticity and honesty in psychoanalytic work.

Fromm did not leave a comprehensive statement of his clinical approach. This has made it difficult for new generations of interpersonal and relational analysts to properly assess his clinical contributions. In our edited book, A Prophetic Analyst: Erich Fromm's Contributions to Psychoanalysis (1996), Michael Maccoby and I have attempted to evaluate Fromm's theoretical and clinical contributions with the hindsight of almost twenty years.

For Fromm, the goal of psychoanalysis is to expand the ground of human freedom by making the unconscious conscious.

We are Delighted to have this opportunity to comment on the work of Benjamin Wolstein and on his very interesting understanding of the psychoanalytic situation and the therapeutic action of psychoanalysis. We also want to express our appreciation and admiration for Irwin Hirsch's masterful interview of Wolstein, who many consider to have been one of the true masters of interpersonal psychoanalysis.

As contemporary Freudian analysts, we have to acknowledge that it took us aback at first to realize that until now we have had almost no exposure to Wolstein's work. One of us had read Fiscalini's chapter on Wolstein in Pioneers of Interpersonal Analysis (Stern, Mann, Kantor & Schlesinger, 1995), but that was all. This lack of familiarity is worthy of note, and so is the fact that when we searched the PEP CD-ROM, which includes the publications through 1994 of five psychoanalytic journals, we found that Wolstein had published forty papers and commentaries in Contemporary Psychoanalysis and none in any of the other four journals (Journal of the American Psychoanalytic Association, Psychoanalytic Quarterly, International Journal of Psycho-Analysis, and Psychoanalytic Study of the Child). Furthermore, there are sixty-one references to Wolstein in Contemporary Psychoanalysis, but only two in JAPA, one in PQ, three in IJP, and none in PSC. The two JAPA citations are by Irwin Hirsch himself. This left us wondering: Did Wolstein ever submit a paper to any of the other four journals? If he did, were they rejected? If he didn't, was it because he thought they would be? Whatever the truth is, the bibliographic facts attest to the great divide that has existed since the 1940s between interpersonal psychoanalysis and the rest of the psychoanalytic world.

I Begin this Article with a vignette about D.W. Winnicott doing an adult consultation that was highly successful. The vignette shows Winnicott working in his inimitable style, which looks easy. Only as one studies the complexity and seriousness of Winnicott's intervention does it becomes clear that his light and playful style emerged from an acute sensitivity to the individual person, as well as to universal aspects of emotional development. The account of the consultation is presented here, both as an example of Winnicott's use of “play” in adult consultation and as a contrast to Masud Khan's play style, which is discussed later.

The vignette comes from Tony Walton,1 a highly acclaimed production designer for movies and Broadway shows and the childhood friend and first husband of actress Julie Andrews. Walton and Andrews had been close friends of Masud Khan and his ballerina wife, Svetlana Beriosova, during the early 1960s. At that time, Khan was in analysis with Winnicott. Walton coincidentally had a consultation with Winnicott in 1965, when Walton and Andrews were ending their marriage.

Timothy Zeddies   psychology resident, University of Texas Health Sciences Center, San Antonio.

The State of Knowledge and authority in psychoanalysis is rapidly expanding and shifting. Postmodernism, hermeneutics, and social constructivism have thoroughly permeated psychoanalytic theory and practice, leading many analytic writers to question, reinterpret, and even dispense with some basic psychoanalytic tenets and assumptions. Traditional psychoanalytic concepts such as neutrality, interpretation, free association, and the unconscious have been dramatically reshaped over the last several decades. This “reshaping” has provoked a crisis of sorts, leaving many analysts scrambling for a stable mooring to ground their identities as analysts.

During this time of transition between paradigms, it is rare to find cogent and illuminating communications that capture the important current difficulties and tensions while providing a way to orient future thinking and practice. In a recent article in this journal, entitled “The Rediscovery of the Unknown: An Inquiry into Psychoanalytic Praxis,” Kenneth Eisold (2000) has offered such a piece. He provides a thoughtful, focused, sensitive, and timely contribution to the ongoing effort of contemporary analytic writers and clinicians to carve out an alternative to objectivism and relativism. He shows that issues related to the unconscious, analytic authority, the therapist's personal influence, and the impact of contrasting interpretive approaches cut across theoretical divides within the psychoanalytic world. More specifically, Eisold points out that in spite of widely divergent interests and approaches proliferating the contemporary psychoanalytic literature, therapists of all stripes continue to struggle with (and often avoid or deny) the unknown—in patients, clinical work, and themselves. He sets out to address this issue by clarifying the nature of analytic work and by sketching a framework for understanding what is meant by the “analytic task.

I Am Very Pleased to have the opportunity to comment on this post-humously published interview. It is a stark reminder of what a brilliant, incisive intellect Ben Wolstein was, and what a loss his death is to the interpersonal tradition and psychoanalysis at large.

Wolstein and I were candidates together at the William Alanson White Institute, and I must confess that I am puzzled by his reference to Clara Thompson as the only influence bearing on him in those days (the early fifties). Those were heady times at White. Although Sullivan had died in 1949, he was still a seminal influence, and Erich Fromm, Fromm-Reichman, Martin Buber, Shunryu Suzuki, Rollo May (invoking existential psychoanalysis and Tillich's theology), were all major influences on us.1 I also know that he was strongly influenced by Edward Tauber, both as a student in his classes and in more personal contacts.2 Moreover, Erwin Singer and I were in joint supervision with Clara Thompson for two years, and although she was an extremely pragmatic and perceptive supervisor, democratic and open to dissent, she was also, in our experience of her in professional and personal contacts, a rather reserved New England lady, not at all revealing of herself. From Hirsch's report, his analysis sounds more like Wolstein teaching Wolstein than Thompson analyzing Wolstein.

The aloneness of the unique self is worlds apart from the loneliness of the relational self.

B. Wolstein

This Year, knee surgery forced upon me a long period of confinement to bed. I was cut off from much of my normal social interaction—the daily give-and-take of meetings, plans with friends, street life. I was not able to busy myself with the innumerable small tasks of household life. For the most part, I saw patients, and then lay in bed, reading and thinking, for six weeks.

I experienced a gamut of states of solitude. I felt extremely anxious, frustrated, and bereft. I was consumed with thoughts of what I was missing. I feared being forgotten. And, to my surprise, I experienced ecstatic and joyful feelings of connection to myself and contentment with just being, a state that my busy life often precludes.

What made the transition from painful “loneliness” to contented “aloneness” possible? And conversely, what made contented “aloneness” dissolve into painful “loneliness” again?

Because I Find Erikson's writing as evocative, inspiring, and clinically useful as any in our field, these two books left me with a feeling of sadness. In the case of Ideas and Identities, the sadness is due to what Robert Wallerstein unflinchingly calls “the psychoanalytic limbo into which Erikson's life work, magisterial as it is, has fallen” (p. 21). It is a limbo from which these essays, interesting as they are and including, as they do, some of Erikson's own best papers, are unlikely to rescue him. No amount of specifying how much Erikson anticipated contemporary thinking can restore to him the currency he has lost. American psychoanalytic history has been told differently, for the most part, and different lineages and loyalties are now in place. My sadness in the case of historian Lawrence Friedman's uninspired biography comes from his carefully documenting, even accentuating, the long years of Erikson's decline. These were years in which his physical and intellectual deterioration were paralleled by his steeply waning significance on the American intellectual scene, where he had achieved more renown than he ever had in strictly psychoanalytic circles. These declines, as psychoanalytic theorist and as cultural eminence, are worth pondering. I focus here more on his decline within psychoanalysis.

Wallerstein and Goldberger's volume builds around five papers from a 1995 San Francisco symposium celebrating the range of Erikson's contributions to various disciplines.

Marcia Cavell offers some thoughts on Erikson's contribution to philosophy. She discusses the contribution of the stage of “autonomy versus shame and doubt” to the development of mind and self.

Neil Smelser provides a thoughtful overview of Erikson's relation to social sciences generally, and to anthropology and history in particular.
